explain.say: In April 1956 an old tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark to Houston carrying 58 metal boxes. Those containers cut loading costs from about 5.86 dollars a ton to about 16 cents. Today's giant ships carry over 20,000 boxes. Look at the timeline of how the world got knitted together, and sometimes torn apart.

explain.say: Now real numbers from the economist Angus Maddison: world exports as a share of world output. About 1 percent in 1820, nearly 8 percent by 1913, the first wave. Then war and depression pulled it back to 5.5 percent in 1950. By 1998 it reached 17 percent. Can you spot the dip, the age of deglobalisation?

What drives each wave? See the reasons. Cheaper transport, faster news, open trade policies, stable money and moving people. The first wave rode steamships, the telegraph and the gold standard; the second rode containers, the internet and new trade rules. Notice that politics can switch it off, as in 1914. Which driver do you think matters most today?

explain.say: Look at the map. The modern artery runs from Shanghai through Singapore and the Suez Canal to Europe. But an older one appears too: from 1571 Spanish galleons carried American silver from Mexico through Manila to China. Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez say global trade was born then. Why would silver matter so much to China?

Now the debate. Historians like Christopher Bayly see long, archaic globalisation; economists Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson say true integration began in the 1820s, when prices started to converge across continents. Brilliant work. Challenge: decide whether today's trade wars are a new deglobalisation.

faq.a: It depends on the definition. Historians such as Christopher Bayly and A. G. Hopkins trace archaic globalisation through the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean; Flynn and Giráldez point to 1571 and the Manila galleons; O'Rourke and Williamson argue real market integration began in the 1820s.
asks: What was the Manila galleon trade?

faq.q: Why did globalisation collapse between 1914 and 1945?
faq.a: Two world wars, the Great Depression, tariffs, the breakdown of the gold standard and migration restrictions cut trade and capital flows. World exports fell from about 9 percent of output in 1929 to about 5.5 percent in 1950.

faq.q: What were the Bretton Woods institutions?
faq.a: Agreed in 1944, they included the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and fixed exchange rates linked to the US dollar. With the 1947 trade agreement GATT, they framed the post-war boom in trade.
asks: What was agreed at Bretton Woods?

faq.q: How did the shipping container change the world?
faq.a: Standard steel boxes, first used on a large scale from 1956, could move from ship to train to truck without unloading. Port costs and theft fell sharply, which made long global supply chains cheap.

faq.q: How much of world output is traded?
faq.a: By Angus Maddison's estimates, world merchandise exports were about 1 percent of world GDP in 1820, 7.9 percent in 1913, 5.5 percent in 1950 and 17.2 percent in 1998.

facts: The Ideal X carried 58 containers from Newark to Houston in April 1956.
Maddison estimated world exports at 7.9 percent of world GDP in 1913 and 5.5 percent in 1950.

quiz.say: World exports were 17.2 percent of output in 1998 and 5.5 percent in 1950. About how many times higher is that?
Which economists argue globalisation truly began in the 1820s?
quiz.why: They use the convergence of prices across continents as their test.

wrong.1: Flynn and Giráldez date it to 1571 and the Manila galleons.
wrong.2: Marx and Engels wrote about world markets but did not set this date.
